title: Electric blanket or heating pad: test it, then take the wire, controller and fleece
summary: An electric blanket or heating pad is a long insulated heating wire sewn through fleece, with a small controller holding a triac or relay, a thermostat and a fuse. Test it first: a working blanket is worth more whole than in parts. A teardown of a dead one takes about 20 minutes with a knife and a meter.

steps.text: Unplug the blanket from the wall, then unplug the controller from the blanket. Look it over: scorch marks, brown or melted patches, kinks, a burnt smell or stiff spots in the fleece all mean the wire has been overheating. Do not power a blanket like that.
steps.warn: A damaged heating wire can overheat and start a fire. Never plug a doubtful blanket in to see if it works.

steps.text: Test it before you cut it. Set the meter to ohms and touch its two probes to the two blanket-side pins of the controller socket (or across the blanket plug). A working mains blanket reads roughly 100–1,100 ohms: a 120 V, 100 W blanket is near 145 ohms and a 230 V, 100 W blanket near 530 ohms (ohms = volts squared divided by watts). No reading means a break or a blown thermal fuse; near zero means a short. A good, undamaged one is better kept whole: it can run from an inverter or a generator.

Controller: undo the screws on the back. Many cases are welded or glued shut: slice the seam with a knife or a thin saw, away from your fingers. Photograph the board and wires before you touch anything.
steps.warn: Even unplugged, a capacitor on the board can still hold a mains-level charge. Short any large one with an insulated resistor lead before you touch the board.

steps.text: Inside you will find a small circuit board with a triac or a relay, a dial or buttons, an indicator lamp and usually a fuse. A triac is a small three-legged part on a metal tab. Desolder the triac, relay, dial, switches and fuse, or cut their legs with 5–10 mm left on.

Thermostat: look for small button thermostats (metal discs, one every 30–40 cm along the wire) and for a second thin sensing wire laid beside the heating wire. Cut each button out with 5 cm of wire. Test one for continuity while it is cold: it should read close to zero ohms.

Heating wire: the wire runs in zigzag channels sewn between the layers of fleece, or is stitched on with thread. Cut the stitches along the channels with a knife, taking care not to cut the wire. Then pull the wire out in long, gentle pulls from the end nearest the cable.

Check the wire. Measure its whole length in ohms and compare with your first reading. Run a finger along it: any kink, bare patch, melted jacket or stiff spot means scrap. Coil good wire loosely in large loops.
Keep the cable and plug. It is a good mains lead: cut the cable at both ends, leaving the plug and a long tail.
Wash the fleece and keep it. With the wire out it is an ordinary blanket, a sleeping bag liner or cloth for insulation, patching or rags.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **A whole working blanket.** It heats a person for about 50–150 W, compared with 1–2 kW for a room heater. Run it from a small inverter or a generator. 12 V car blankets draw 40–60 W (about 4–5 A) straight from a battery: fit a 7.5–10 A fuse in the lead.
- **Triac and dimmer.** A triac with its dial makes a simple mains dimmer for heaters and incandescent lamps. Don't use it on motors or LED lamps. Check its ratings on the part or the circuit board.
- **Thermostats and fuse.** Small button thermostats and thermal fuses are useful anywhere you need an overheat cutoff.
- **Heating wire.** Keep it at its original length and voltage. Its resistance is fixed per metre, so power is voltage squared divided by resistance. A mains blanket wire at 12 V gives about 1 W: useless. If you cut it shorter and run it at its mains voltage, the power per metre rises and the insulation melts.
- **Fleece.** Insulation and lining.

## Rules for reusing the wire

- Don't splice or shorten mains heating wire. A joint can overheat and a short length cannot shed its heat.
- Don't bundle, bury or cover live wire; a blanket works only because the heat spreads.
- Run it only with its own thermostat or a fuse in line.

## Variations

- 12 V and 24 V blankets and low-voltage pads use a thicker wire with fewer ohms. They may have no controller at all, just a switch.
- Some low-voltage blankets use a transformer in the plug. Keep it: it is a small mains transformer.
- Heating pads often have a thin sensing wire in addition to the heater, and a digital controller with a small microcontroller board.

## What to leave

- A blanket wire that is kinked, scorched or stiff.
- Controllers that smell burnt.
